19505:
I added an Astrovision Inc. press release from September 1980. The title of the release is "Astrovision Acquires Bally's Consumer Products Division: New Marketing Drive Planned for Home 'Bally Professional Arcade.'"

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/press/press.html#Astrovision_Inc_Press_Release_Sept_1980

This press release is from September 29, 1980, making it the earliest press release I've seen from Astrovision.  Most of the others are from June 1982.  It announces the re-release of the Bally Professional Arcade. This was sent by Astrovision to James Costello at Golden West Sales, Inc., a BPA distributor, I think, who passed it on to Bob Fabris, the editor of the Arcadian newsletter. There are two additional pages included in this document: a short letter to Bob from James and another, full-page letter, from Astrovision to James.

I OCRed this press release, but not the two letters in this document.  The press release is available in text format on the website, but I'm including it here (see below) too.

Highlights that you'll find in this press release are the idea that the system will be marketed in Europe and Latin America.  Also, according to the announcement, only 14 cartridges were available for the system at the time.  This console's library sure was small.  It's no wonder that people resorted to making and distributing games on tape for BASIC.

Enjoy!

Adam

(This is the press release:)

--------------------

Astrovision Acquires Bally's Consumer Products Division:
New Marketing Drive Planned for Home 'Bally Professional Arcade'

(Sept. 1980)

COLUMBUS, OHIO --- Astrovision, Inc., a Columbus-based electronics firm is mounting a three-pronged marketing and manufacturing drive for the 'Bally Professional Arcade'. Astrovision purchased the consumer products division of Bally Manufacturing Corp. in August.

The 'Bally Professional Arcade', with 14 cassettes and 28 existing games and educational programs, is the most technically sophisticated home electronic video game center available. It is the only such unit with programming capabilities which through the addition of a low cost add-on feature, called BASIC with an audio interface, expands capabilities for self-teaching and other uses.

"Astrovision's plans for the 'Bally Professional Arcade' include an international marketing thrust into Europe and Latin America, the introduction of seven to nine, new 'Videocade' cassettes, and the introduction of an add-on keyboard to make existing 'Bally Professional Arcade' units into full scale home computer systems," Dan Dawson, Astrovision vice president stated.

"Astrovision will position the 'Bally Professional Arcade' as a complete home computer system with state-of-the-art games plus all at-home needs," Dawson continued.

Astrovision will introduce a new 'Videocade' cassette named "Dogpatch" in time for Christmas, 1980 sales and will launch six to eight additional cassettes with new programming in 1981. These cassettes will include the long sought-after second generation space invader game.

The full scale add-on keyboard will also be available in 1981, according to Dawson.

"The 'Bally Professional Arcade' today is far more than a game machine. It offers basic programming capabilities with the "Brain", a powerful microprocessor that creates a memory bank and which holds more than 12,000 instructions, even before a cassette is inserted. Each unit includes skill games such as Checkmate, Gunfight and Scribbling and features a full five function, ten key memory calculator," Dawson said. "With the add-on keyboard scheduled for 1981, the 'Bally Professional Arcade' will be a complete home video computer center offering versatile family entertainment plus vital bookkeeping, business management and household management programs."

Games and educational programs currently offered for the 'Bally Professional Arcade' include: 280Zzzap, Bally Pin, Sea Wolf, Red Baron, Football, Tornado Baseball, Star Battle, Astro Battle a space invader game, Amazin' Maze, Tic-Tac-Toe, Black Jack, Poker, Acey Ducey, Dodgem, Missile, Panzer Attack, Brickyard, Clowns, Tennis, Hockey, Handball, Bingo Math, Speed Math, Letter Match, Spell 'N' Score, Crosswords and BASIC.

BASIC, a unique feature for the 'Bally Professional Arcade' permits the user to create his own programs. It provides an entire library of video games, art, music and more, plus a self-teaching course that lets users develop programs in minutes.

The 'Bally Professional Arcade' will be available through Montgomery Ward stores and other leading retailers. For further information contact: Astrovision, Inc., 6460 Busch Blvd., Suite 215, in Columbus, Ohio 43229, 800-848-4377.

'Bally Professional Arcade' units will have a suggested retail price of about $299 with cassette programs at $19.95 and $24.95.

I added the Bally Professional Arcade promotional newspaper/catalog from 1978.

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/marketing_materials/marketing_materials.html#Bally_Professional_Arcade_Promotional_Newspaper-Catalog

This large-format, 16-page promotional advertisement, in the format of a newspaper, explains, in detail, the features of the Bally Professional Arcade and contains the entire manual for Bally BASIC. This must be an early promotional/catalog, as NCE/Compumart Inc. stopped carrying the Bally Arcade on December 1, 1978, as reported in ARCADIAN 1, no. 2 (Dec. 4, 1978): 1.  In this same issue of the Arcadian, which is only the second subscriber issue of the newsletter, it is already rumored that Bally is pulling out of the market after shipping the first consoles in January of 1978.  That didn't take long, did it?

This newspaper-size ad was much too large to fit on my scanner. I took pictures of it, which are quite inferior to a quality scanned document. The default download link is hardly readable. I've included a 30MB pdf too that is only slightly-more readable.


I like this catalog so much that I've attached a jpg image of it to this post to give you a better idea of what to expect from the pdf.  If I got this catalog for free in the mail in 1978, I would have wanted this system!

In August of 2002, I asked if anyone remembered this Compumart company, here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/76318057#17365

Compumart also pops up in an article called "Bally Professional Arcade" by Karl Zimm published in "Creative Computing," 4, no. 5 (Sept-Oct 1978): 56-59.

and here:

https://ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/Bally%20Professional%20Arcade/Bally%20Professional%20Arcade%20(Sept-Oct%201978)(Karl%20Zinn)(Creative%20Computing).pdf

The 8.5 x 8.5" low/hi-res screen SRAM Board 1 has been tested to run perfect with SRAM of various access times: 75, 85, 100, 120 and 150ns. The board runs perfect in low and hi-res.

MCM plans to record a video demonstrating BD1, once the newly revised low-res only screen SRAM scheme plus the quick-connect composite video/audio drivers scheme are wire wrapped on Vector boards. How long will it take to WW these 2 boards? Not sure, 5 weeks, maybe longer.

MCM is planning to WW a backup BD1 as a test for compatibility and as a quick check diagnostic tool.

A fourth Astrocade motherboard MIGHT be modified for hi-res as a final test for compatibility.

The second modified for hi-res Astrocade motherboard has a failure on it and needs to be diagnosed.

The hi-res schematic DWGs 2, 3 and 4 archived on the Bally Alley should now be considered OBSOLETE (having limited compatibility). A bunch of improvements have been made on BD1. These DWGs should really be deleted from the website, to eventually be replaced with newly revised DWGs 1 thru 6, which will include a revision number.

FYI, the 8KB BalcheckHR program package includes 3 hi-res graphic demos listed below:

Move Critter, Wagon and Fish (original hi-res demo)
Textured 10 Color Test Pattern Variation
The Pixel Stringer

Note that a low/hi-res software select scheme is required to run these 3 programs. They are not accessible using a manual low/hi-res mini-toggle switch.

The BalcheckHR bin file and source code are archived on the Bally Alley. The source code includes extensive program comments.

Two other hi-res programs are also included with BalcheckHR:

Hi-Res SetScreen2
Hi-Res Screen RAM Test Program (similar to the low-res Balcheck screen RAM test).
Both programs require the use of a dual 7-segment display to report specific diagnostic info.

Finally, the entire BalcheckHR package will run in hi-res by changing only 13 bytes within the 8KB coding. This change is documented in the BalcheckHR User Manual. Low-res graphics will be displayed only within the top 1/4 (4000-4FFFH) area of the hi-res display. Because of the way the hi-res screen RAM is mapped, the low-res graphics will be split in two, on the left and the right sides.

End Of Report 5
MCM Design

19541:
Ken's posting #19534 indicated relating to my testing of the low/hi-res screen RAM BD1 using 70, 85, 100, 120 and 150ns SRAM,
"Consider the fact that the first Bally's were run on 450uS DRAMS, almost any SRAM now will blow that timing out of the water".

You were careful to suggest that ALMOST any SRAM speed would work on my BD1 scheme.

Not to long ago, I breadboarded a "low-res only" SRAM scheme using the same DRAM interfacing scheme utilized on the Astrocade motherboard.

This breadboard would connect to my "modified for hi-res" Astrocade motherboard, which has a 28 pin DIL connector mounted on it. The connector has 28 tapped motherboard signal lines wired to it.

The breadboard generated the active low CS/RAS, CAS, WE lines and had access to the DATEN line, nearly identical to the same motherboard DRAM control lines. No 2K pull-up resistors were used. Also, there were no 1K pull-ups on the load side of U20 (74LS174) for the RAM A0-A5 lines.

All I had to add to complete the SRAM interfacing scheme was a 74LS373 to latch in the SRAM row address.

I tried SRAM with a 120ns and 70ns access time. This low-res SRAM scheme worked perfect.

However, when I used a narrow package Cypress CY7C185 8KB SRAM with a 15ns access time, the SRAM scheme would not work right.

I ran my Z80 Check and Fill Screen Write programs. These 2 programs only write graphics to screen RAM. The Z80 does not read screen RAM or utilize a stack area in it. It was obvious that the Z80 had some kind of an issue writing to this faster SRAM chip.

I did not spend any time to determine if there was also a read issue with this faster chip. I may spend some time later trying to determine the cause of this write issue. Maybe my logic analyzer might reveal something.

Any idea Ken why this 15ns SRAM chip is not operating perfect? I triple checked the wiring to the chip.

The breadboarded low-res SRAM interfacing scheme described above is implying that the Astrocade motherboard U23 (DM81LS95) and 8 DRAM chips can be replaced with only a 74LS373 and one SRAM chip. All the RAM interfacing lines can be taken from the U23 and U24 (DRAM) solder pads, including the +5v and gnd lines. A DIL pc socket could be soldered onto each of these 2 solder patterns. This would provide a quick connect for a small pc board with a 74LS373 and one SRAM plus 2 DIL ribbon cable plugs on it. This pc board would sit on top of the motherboard were the 8 DRAM chips use to be. You might have to remove the 9 motherboard pull-up resistors.

I may later test this implication on one of my "modified for hi-res" Astrocade motherboards.

When I first breadboarded my low/hi-res SRAM scheme, I was using only 120ns SRAM. The scheme was working perfect in low and hi-res.

Then later, I found out my low/hi-res SRAM scheme wouldn't work right using faster SRAM. If I recall correctly, the scheme had an issue with a 100ns SRAM.

So, I was forced to return to my breadboard and had to revise the scheme, so it would run my 70, 85 and 100ns SRAM perfect in low and hi-res.

I have added a better grayscale scan of "Facts and Figures about the BPA: Facts and Figures about the Bally Professional Arcade and Computer Add-On." This 16-page document was published by Bally Consumer Products Division in about 1978. It is form FCPR-0-8008-0400.  I consider this a must-read document:

You can read it here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/marketing_materials/marketing_materials.html#Facts_and_Figures_BPA_and_Add-On

I originally posted this document on January 27, 2010.  There was some discussion about it at that time from Lance Squire, Bill Loguidice, Ken Lill, and Brett Bilbrey, who commented, "In other news [here at Apple]... Today has been a busy day here with our iPad announcement. My group was responsible for the first prototype. ;-)"

Here is the archived thread on Groups.io about my original post about the "Facts and Figures" document:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/54290489#8110

Today, I OCRed the first two pages of the document:

--------------------

About Our New Computer

The big question that just about everybody asks is "Why so cheap? How can a home computer with so much power cost so little while the other units on the market cost so much?"

The answer lies in a phenomenon that is unique to computers and that Bally recognized early. Integrated circuits generally represent only about 10% of the cost of most home computers. The bulk of the other costs are in software-- the cost of man hours or man years required to program the computer to make it easy to operate and useful for different applications. In fact, more than 50% of the cost of a computer is the software that went into it and not the hardware, as is the case with most other products.

If half the cost of a home computer is the cost of software, it is usually based on the sale of a few thousand units. If sales are doubled, then software represents 25% of the cost and the rest is reflected in profit. So the more units sold, the less the actual cost of software per unit to the manufacturer. Unlike mass production cost savings, there's always a basic cost of materials to consider no matter how much is produced, but not so with software. Produce twice as much and your costs are halved.

So Bally's strategy was to produce a home computer in three steps, the first step containing practically all the software in the form of a TV game that would appeal to a mass consumer audience that will be expandable into a home computer. Second, with an additional purchase of our Bally Basic Cassette, the calculator keypad is transformed into an alpha-numeric keypad which enables you to write programs up to 1800 characters. We feel this to be the best way to familiarize the public with programming in the BASIC language. The third step will be the purchase of our keyboard add-on which will contain the complementary components to increase the unit's power into a complete home or business computer.

The TV game can be sold in huge quantities to a mass audience and thus the cost of the software per unit is very low. By also designing the TV game for an expansion module, the total cost of the entire package is also very low. The end result is the highest quality TV game on the market with the quality standards and total memory power of a home computer plus the ability to expand the TV game into a home computer with software and hardware supplied by Bally.

This rare combination means that a very extensive software package represents as little as 5% of the total cost of the unit, and the integrated circuits represent over 30% of the cost.

The results provide a unique opportunity to buy a product that is not only the lowest priced system available, but is also the best-- and fully expandable through additional inexpensive modules. Your unit will keep step with advancing technology.

In the comparison sheet located in the center of this book, we have listed our personal computer with part of the add-on module. The video display or digital cassette deck is not included in order to make a fair comparison with the other units.

--------------------

So much of this document never came to be completed in the unit that was finally sold. Never mind what was never released (the computer add-on), but even simple facts in this document are wrong or misleading. For instance, the stated speed of the tape interface is 4,800-BAUD, but it was released as 300-BAUD: quite a difference. It's no wonder that the first wave of Bally Arcade owners felt like they had been lied to about what they would get.

1) About Our New Computer
2) Software
3) Hardware
4) Hardware Comparision Chart
5) Questions and Answers

19563:
On October 26, 2022, Allen Schweitzer wrote, "the only surprise to me (about the astrocade in general) is that the game can be switched out with the system on. does it shadow the ROM into RAM or something on boot?"

The Astrocade does not shadow its ROM into RAM at any time.  Heck, there isn't even the room for it.  The ROM is 8K and there is only 4K of RAM, all of which is screen RAM.  The poor ROM has nowhere to go.

The carts are grounded and can be removed and then another one can placed into the system with the console still turned on.  However, afterward, the Reset button must be pressed to get the new cartridge to be seen on the menu.  Later, the trick used by BASICarts was created to switch carts without needing to press the Reset button.  I mostly understand how this works; the system is put into a tight loop and then the user presses a keypad button to break the loop, in which case the program continues running.

Ken Lill can probably explain some of the work-arounds to copy the ROM to RAM, as some hardware, such as the 64K RAM board, does allow for this function to be used using DIP switches.  Heck, even Ken's own Lil' Red Ram (never produced) was going to allow for this function.

I added the 300-BAUD version of "Air/Sea Battle" for Bally BASIC by an unknown author to BallyAlley.com.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#Air-Sea_Battle_Bally_BASIC

This is a previously unknown amateur program. Paul says, "This game is like the Atari 2600 cartridge, but it is extremely slow."  First, to say this game is "slow" is somewhat of an understatement.  Please, forgive it, as it was never meant to be seen by anyone except the author.  Also, except in name, this game isn't much like Air/Sea Battle, as it's far too primitive.


Although this game isn't fun, I don't think it was meant to be exciting.  Rather, I suspect it was a programming exercise for someone learning BASIC because the program is heavily commented.  I suspect that just removing the comments would speed up this game enough to make it semi-playable.  As it is now, it's not tolerable enough to finish one round of gameplay.  Also, I was never able to hit a target.  I have attached the BASIC listing of this game below.  Check it out; do you think it was meant to be a finished game?

19584:
On October 30, 2022, David Kindred wrote, "Thanks for continuing to post such interesting things, Adam."

Yeah, it's been fun posting again to the Bally Alley website.  There is so much interesting material in the BallyAlley archives that needs to be added to the website.  Nearly all of it is available in a few downloads on archive.org, here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/Archives/Archives.html

Adding the information to my Astrocade site a little at a time, and with context, makes it more fun for me, and, I hope, for the readers of these posts.

I have a bit of extra information about Herb, the person who put his Bally Arcade into the blue case with a keyboard.  On the first page of the March 1979 issue, Bob Fabris writes:

"LETTERHEAD of this issue was donated by Herb Weintraub. It is an interesting idea..."

This is from ARCADIAN 1, no. 5 (Mar. 23, 1979): 31.  You can see the letterhead in this issue:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_1/arcadian_vol_1_issue_05.pdf

Bob did use this letterhead for the rest of volume 1.  Volume 2 began with the November 1979 issue (ARCADIAN 2, no. 1 (Nov. 29, 1979): 1-8.).  This is the first issue with the new Arcadian Logo letterhead that stuck around until the end of the Arcadian's seven-volume run into 1986:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_2/arcadian_vol_02_issue_01.pdf

This "Arcadian Logo" is by Guy McLimore and appears in a program in Arcadian 2, no. 1 (Nov. 29, 1979): 3.  These notes were included:

"Logo shown at the head of page one is based on an idea by Guy McLimore, and embellished by myself. If you'd like to see it in action (literally) and in living color, the program is included."

Here is a link to the AstroBASIC program:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#ArcadianLogoGuyMcLimoreAB

It's great that Bob had so much input from the readers of his newsletter.  It's these readers collective works that make the history of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade so intriguing to me and, I believe, to some extent, to all Astrocade fans.

I've uploaded Arcadian compilation tapes produced by Richard Houser. Thanks to Nate Reeder for loaning these out. While I didn't find new programs on these, I hadn't previously seen the index and instructions, and a tape can't really be considered completely archived without any documentation that was released alongside it.

https://archive.org/details/richard-houser-arcadian-compilation-tapes/

The Arcadian newsletter published BASIC programs and other information regarding the Bally Professional Arcade / Astrocade game console. While these could be typed in from the published listings, Richard Houser also sold compilation tapes with the published programs for easy loading. These two tapes cover volumes 1 and 2, published from 1978 to 1980. The recordings are in the the 300 baud format used with the original version of the Bally BASIC cartridge and an external interface for loading.

I've previously archived another copy of these tapes on www.ballyalley.com, so I haven't digitally processed these, but I'm uploading the raw recordings and scans of the tapes, cases, and an example of the insert used. Also included are scans of the index and instructions which came with the tapes, which had not been seen before.

Paul

Subject: Five New Bally (Nitron) Documents Uploaded
Date: April 15, 2006
Sent by Adam Trionfo

I've uploaded to Ballyalley.com some new documents on the Bally Professional Arcade that I've placed in a new section called "Nitron."  These historical documents show the end of the line for Nitron, the company that worked with Astrovision to produce the Astrocade.

The five documents are:

1) Everything Must Go! - No Date - This is it. Nitron loses their lease and they must liquidate everything.

2) Final Inventory Letter - 11/14/1984 - The company is so out of money that they don't have cash to send flyers to customers. It's a sad thing to see a company fall.

3) Addendum Prices - 12/06/1984 - The end was in sight! They began to cut the prices of the cartridges even more (though only by 10%). They also started to offer a package deal where if you bought a system then you would get twenty-four cartridges with it, all for $199.95

4) Final Inventory - 01/07/1984 - This sheet shows how many cartridges and Astrocades that Nitron still had in inventory right at the end. There isn't nearly as many as I expected, most cartridges are under one-thousand left (though Galactic Invasion still had 18,000). There are 857 Astrocades left; no wonder they're so rare!

5) Auction Announcement 03/13/1985 - This appeared in the San Jose Mercury News.  Not only was the inventory being sold off, but the whole facility was auctioned as well!

You can download them here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/misc_docs/nitron/nitron.html

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/nitron/nitron.html

To me, the whole Nitron part of the Astrocade story was always a little confusing to me.  This sheds a little light onto the end of the subject.

There are a few other Nitron documents already online at Ballyalley.com that I'm eventually going to consolidate into this area.

Adam

I've uploaded to Ballyalley.com some new documents on the Bally Professional Arcade that I've placed in a new section called "Nitron."  These historical documents show the end of the line for Nitron, the company that worked with Astrovision to produce the Astrocade.

The five documents are:

1) Everything Must Go! - No Date - This is it. Nitron loses their lease and they must liquidate everything.

2) Final Inventory Letter - 11/14/1984 - The company is so out of money that they don't have cash to send flyers to customers. It's a sad thing to see a company fall.

3) Addendum Prices - 12/06/1984 - The end was in sight! They began to cut the prices of the cartridges even more (though only by 10%). They also started to offer a package deal where if you bought a system then you would get twenty-four cartridges with it, all for $199.95

4) Final Inventory - 01/07/1984 - This sheet shows how many cartridges and Astrocades that Nitron still had in inventory right at the end. There isn't nearly as many as I expected, most cartridges are under one-thousand left (though Galactic Invasion still had 18,000). There are 857 Astrocades left; no wonder they're so rare!

5) Auction Announcement 03/13/1985 - This appeared in the San Jose Mercury News.  Not only was the inventory being sold off, but the whole facility was auctioned as well!

You can download them here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/misc_docs/nitron/nitron.html
https://ballyalley.com/documentation/nitron/nitron.html

To me, the whole Nitron part of the Astrocade story was always a little confusing to me.  This sheds a little light onto the end of the subject.

There are a few other Nitron documents already online at Ballyalley.com that I'm eventually going to consolidate into this area.

Adam

I'm as little confused as to the exact arrangement between Astrocade and Nitron. "Bernstein Research - The Video Game Industry" by Christopher Kirby (Dec. 28, 1982) says Astrocade was recently acquired by Nitron. I think this might be an oversimplification. Arcadian volume 4 v 11 page 113 describes an odd arrangement where Nitron purchased inventory from Astrocade and would then use the inventory for manufacturing systems and cartridges to then sell back to Astrocade. Bob Fabris later described this as follows:
"Early in 1982, Nitron of Cupertino, California became another player in the Astrocade group. In June, it became the principal supplier of hardware to Astrocade. In a rather unusual arrangement, Nitron bought Astrocade's entire arcade, cartridge and component inventory, contracting to purchase component parts (the major chips were sole-sourced from American Microsystems). Nitron then assembled the gear and sold it back to Astrocade. The purchase gave Astrocade some needed cash but made it highly dependent on Nitron's performance. Some Bay Area subscribers and I visited the facility and were impressed to see that Nitron apparently had all of the necessary equipment and capabilities to complete all of the required work under one roof (although the Garner and Sacramento plants were to continue their efforts, with Nitron as overseer)."
https://ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/Robert_Fabris_introduction-edited.html


The article in the Sept. 1983 issue of Semiconductor International says Nitron is "attempting to acquire" Astrocade.
Are there any other references to Nitron acquiring Astrocade?

In summary, as of 1978, what you'll discover is that the following model numbers each have a meaning:

I'm the one who made that forum thread!
The Bally Arcade core on Mister is all right, but it's one of the earlier ones that were ported to the project and as such is missing a lot of QoL features later cores from the same developer have (like a composite filter, off the top of my head). Additionally, she wasn't aware that the Bally had cassette interfaces or RAM expansions, so the core does not have those implemented. She indicated to me that they'd be relatively easy to add with schematics (Which I did provide) but that she wasn't sure when she'd be able to loop back around to the core. To my knowledge, no one else has taken those up. There's no reason why it couldn't run BASIC programs as wav files or as binaries, technically speaking, and one of the optional items for a Mister is the audio jack for cassette-based platforms, so you could in theory load those up the same way if the core had support added.
I do know a developer currently working on some 1970s arcade games, I may see if he'd be interested/able to take a crack at adding those Bally Arcade features when he's got a chance.

19615:
On November 5, 2022, Paul Thacker wrote, "[In this WIP of Laser Battle, the] tank on the right doesn't seem to fire. [...] It's a nice concept. Either tank can move up or down. When the tank on the left fires, it first breaks a gap in the shield on the right, then can pass through to the tank the next shot. If it fires too often, it needs to pause to reload."

Paul's archiving post caught my interest, so I loaded the 300-baud "Laser Battle" game onto my real Astrocade, as 300-Baud programs can't be loaded using emulation in MAME.  The game takes about three minutes to load.  All the while, as the BASIC lines are listed to the screen, it can be seen that the lines are full of code, unlike the Doug Shaeffer programs that Chris and I loaded last week, which consisted of one BASIC command per logical line.  This program runs fine, but, as Paul says, the tank on the right can't fire its cannon.

I've attached five pictures of the game being played.  Perhaps this will arouse someone's interest to help Paul find the bug in the program that doesn't allow the right tank to fire at the left player.

This game, while not ultra fast (it's BASIC, after all) plays quickly and draws the graphics faster than Shaeffer's "Star Wars" and "Cross Country Racer" games.  Then again, Super Software released games that were sold commercially, while Shaeffer's games were programmed solely for himself.  Also, I like the sound effects in this game.  The drawing of the exploding tank is also effective for a game written in BASIC.  Programmers sure used the BOX command to great effect.

I still find it wonderful that 1.8K of RAM, just a few dozen lines of code, could allow fun programs to be made on the Astrocade using Bally BASIC.  And yet... have I made a game using Bally BASIC yet?  Nope.  [Adam drops his eyes slowly, sighs deeply, and thinks to himself, "Someday... ah, someday...]

Adam

19620: Adam wanted me to share a story with the group of how I spent my Saturday (yesterday).  A customer who bought a console off e-bay from me sent me a package that arrived last Wednesday.  Inside were 3 Bally consoles - all in non-working condition.  2 had bad RAM's and the 3rd had bad capacitors.  I got them all working on the same day!  I wish I had that good of luck with every console I worked on, but I'm slowly getting better with time.  He also included 3 controllers with flaky pots.  I fixed them up like new, so another happy customer!One day I'd like to do a video of a controller repair, but I don't have the equipment or knowledge of how to do video's and post them.  Maybe that should be my next project.  I have quite a system for pot repairs that really seems to hold up.  I have had a customer contact me years after buying from me to tell me the pots were working just as good as the day he bought them from me.I use 5 chemicals when I take the pot completely apart and refurb it.  Trial and error over the years and fixing who knows how many controllers has proven this system works great!Step 1 - Clean the resistor plate (and contacts) with acetoneStep 2 - Everclear to remove the acetone residue (I only use Everclear as it leaves no residue)Step 3 - Goo Gone gets the rest of it and leaves a slight oily film on the resistor plate.  I actually leave a certain amount on there.Step 4 and 5 - BARELY a dab of di-electric grease and white lithium grease at 10 and 2, with 6 being the bottom, or "stopper" on the pot.  Too much of either, and you're running a risk that it will jitter.  It actually doesn't take as long as it sounds, but it doesn't work every time.  Some pots just will not take, and some will not come apart...mostly the ones with the flat bottom.  For those, a pipe cleaner works good.  On the others, a q-tip.  For those "detoxit" sprayers out there, I'm sure your system works too, but I haven't had good luck with that being a fix that lasts very long.It also helps that Ken Lill bought me a pair of extreme magnification glasses that REALLY show any bits of "hair" on the pot.  Not sure how strands of dust get inside the pot, but after 40+ years I guess anything is possible.  The cleanest of pots will jitter if there is a thin little strand of fabric hair on the contacts or touching the resistor plate.Anyway, it was good to see 3 units (and 3 controllers) come to life for me on a Saturday!  :)

I don't know about that, but a map would definitely be advisable, especially since the navigation seems to be pretty random rather than like an actual physical space.

I started my YouTube channel with just my phone. At the time it was a
Samsung Galaxy S7. I got a small "cheap" tripod, microphone and phone mount
for it.

Then I got a used GoPro3 that stopped working shortly after I got it (fell
off my quad and got ran over on the way back from filming my first video
with it), but It came with the GoPro Studio software. I used that to put my
videos together. That software is no longer supported and I've not had any
luck using it with 4K video, so I now use OpenShot video editor (Free).
There is a little bit of a learning curve, but it's fairly easy to figure
out.

You could also use OBS Studio (Free) on your computer if it has a webcam on
it. Then you wouldn't need to get anything, just a bit of setup is all.

You could do a 'live YouTube broadcast' and it should save on you channel.
Just let all of us know ahead of time when your going to do it so we can
all sit in and watch! :D

I now use a GoPro 10, and have a few different tripods and such. I did just
finally get an LED light that I can mount on either a tripod or the cold
shoe on the GoPro. I also just got new microphones (old ones were poop).

That being said, you really don't need any of that, just a phone, tripod
and a way to put your video together.

Also, You don't need a 'script', but it does help to have a que card of
some sort, just with bullet points of things you want to say or show. Once
I start filming, sometimes I 'forget' to say something or spend more time
on something I wanted to show. I also put on my que card in bold large
sharpie to 'STOP RAMBLING' Lol. That way I don't have to edit that out.

 Adam wanted me to share a story with the group of how I spent my Saturday (yesterday).  A customer who bought a console off e-bay from me sent me a package that arrived last Wednesday.  Inside were 3 Bally consoles - all in non-working condition.  2 had bad RAM's and the 3rd had bad capacitors.  I got them all working on the same day!  I wish I had that good of luck with every console I worked on, but I'm slowly getting better with time.  He also included 3 controllers with flaky pots.  I fixed them up like new, so another happy customer!One day I'd like to do a video of a controller repair, but I don't have the equipment or knowledge of how to do video's and post them.  Maybe that should be my next project.  I have quite a system for pot repairs that really seems to hold up.  I have had a customer contact me years after buying from me to tell me the pots were working just as good as the day he bought them from me.I use 5 chemicals when I take the pot completely apart and refurb it.  Trial and error over the years and fixing who knows how many controllers has proven this system works great!Step 1 - Clean the resistor plate (and contacts) with acetoneStep 2 - Everclear to remove the acetone residue (I only use Everclear as it leaves no residue)Step 3 - Goo Gone gets the rest of it and leaves a slight oily film on the resistor plate.  I actually leave a certain amount on there.Step 4 and 5 - BARELY a dab of di-electric grease and white lithium grease at 10 and 2, with 6 being the bottom, or "stopper" on the pot.  Too much of either, and you're running a risk that it will jitter.  It actually doesn't take as long as it sounds, but it doesn't work every time.  Some pots just will not take, and some will not come apart...mostly the ones with the flat bottom.  For those, a pipe cleaner works good.  On the others, a q-tip.  For those "detoxit" sprayers out there, I'm sure your system works too, but I haven't had good luck with that being a fix that lasts very long.It also helps that Ken Lill bought me a pair of extreme magnification glasses that REALLY show any bits of "hair" on the pot.  Not sure how strands of dust get inside the pot, but after 40+ years I guess anything is possible.  The cleanest of pots will jitter if there is a thin little strand of fabric hair on the contacts or touching the resistor plate.Anyway, it was good to see 3 units (and 3 controllers) come to life for me on a Saturday!  :)

The main problem here is that the ":..."info is not going to the line input buffer. When you save it to tape and have the :INPUT or :RUN or :INPUT;RUN in the command line when saving, it loads that command into the line input buffer and then when you load it in, it executes that command. You'll need to go back to some of the early Arcadian program tips to get all of the info as hot to do it correctly.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#LifeSynthesisModelBBFredCornett

The full documentation, including a complete explanation and breakdown of the program, a "Starter Colony Location Grid" and a "Sample Starter Colony" are available in the Cursor newsletter.  Part of the documentation is included here to get you started with this program.

The rules are Simple:

1. Survival. Every cell with 2 or 3 adjacent cells survives for the next generation.

2. Death. Each cell with 4 or more neighbors dies from overpopulation. Every cell with 1 neighbor or none dies from isolation.

3. Births. Each empty cell adjacent to exactly 3 live cells is a birth cell.

Using the grid supplied, plot the location of your starter colony. Best results are obtained by keeping the cells in one area. After inputting the starter colony, the computer will search the complete field, taking approximately 25 minutes. This will occur only during generation #1, on subsequent generations, the computer will only search those quadrants where life exists.

Please note the "search locators" on the top and left side of the field border. The locators will show you where the computer is currently performing a search.

19665:
Quick-Connect Composite Video and Audio Drivers Board Replaces Astec RF Modulator
Nov 2022

The Astrocade's Astec RF modulator utilizes the LM1889 TV video modulator chip. Fortunately, all of the electronic RF components within the LM1889 scheme can be removed and still generate a composite video colored output.

Seventeen resistor and capacitor (RC) components in the LM1889 scheme help process 5 video related signal lines from the Astrocade motherboard, fed to the Astec modulator via a quick-connect 8 pin connector. There are an additional 7 RC processing components near the motherboard's custom data chip, which are also connected to the 5 video related lines.

The 8 pin connector also provides +10v, -5v power lines plus an audio output line. The underside of the Astec metal case is grounded to the Astrocade motherboard via a copper flex connector attached to the Astrocade's bottom RF shielding, which is fastened using tiny screws to the motherboard gnd contacts.

MCM Design has bread boarded, tested and wire wrapped a quick-connect board which includes:

17 RC component LM1889 video processing scheme
composite video driver
audio driver
3.5 mm audio/video output jack.

Rather than describe this board, attached to this posting are 4 photos and 2 electronic schematics.

The A/V board has room to accommodate one of 2 options for a video driver:

Option 1     The surface mounted THS7314 driver,
Option 2     Datamax UV-1R two-transistor configuration driver.

The THS7314 option is already posted on the Bally Alley website in the Miscellaneous Hardware Documents section.

Which video driver is the better choice?

The THS7314 driver might be a little clearer. The comparison is too close to determine which option is visually better. One obvious distinction was observed. The THS7314 driver displayed the somewhat transparent bottom text in the Astrocade Menu, differently.

ADDITIONAL COMMENTS:

1. The LM1889 scheme has some TV display graphic issues. For example, in Checkmate, there typically is a narrow white line along the top and sides of the score fields and the play area. The 2 video drivers documented in this report will NOT correct the already existing graphic issues generated by the LM1889 scheme.

2. An audio driver was included to help protect the custom I/O chip, should the audio cable accidentally be plugged into an OUTPUT jack on a TV or remote audio amplifier.

3. The audio video output jack faces the left side of the Astrocade instead of its back, which means the left side of the Astrocade console must have an opening to accommodate the A/V cable. This choice was made because MCM Design's final hi-res Astrocade console will have a keyboard connector mounted on the left side and near the back to accommodate an upgraded 24-key keyboard that will be located in front of the Astrocade.

4. Video driver transistors can NOT be plugged directly into a breadboard. Apparently, the underlying breadboard contacts affect the transistors video performance (incorrect colors). Instead, the transistors must be hard wired onto a tiny Vector Board, then placed on top of the breadboard.

5.
Tested substitutions for 1st choice MPSH69 PNP transistor
2N3906  ok
2N4125  ok
NTE159  no, slightly blurry text/graphics

Tested substitutions for 1st choice 2N4401 NPN transistor
2N3904  ok
2N4123  ok
TP3565  ok
MPS5179  ok

6. To lower the risk of line noise:
The LM1889 chip was located close to the Astrocade 8 pin connector.
The A/V output jack was located close to the video driver output line.

7. For the LM1889 scheme, because one .02uf cap was missing in MCM Design's inventory, two .01uf caps were wired in parallel.

8. The LM386N chip has a very low output impedance, capable of driving an 8 ohm speaker. The A/V board's audio output line was surprisingly very quiet (in most cases, no line noise when hooked up to a 20" Toshiba CRT TV) any time the Astrocade did not output any sound.

9. The A/V board gnd can be connected to the Astrocade motherboard gnd using a wire with a small alligator clip.

10. The THS7314 chip, at this time, is in stock at Mouser Electronics, part# 595–THS7314D.

End Of Posting
MCM Design

"Dodge heat-seeking missiles and outdraw the sinister mechanoids as you seek to win back your planet."

I've attached a screenshot and ad for this game.  This archive includes two screenshots of the game (one from the MAME emulator and one from real hardware), a review of Tape 103 from 1983, and an ad for Tape 103 that appeared in the June 1982 "Arcadian" newsletter, featuring "Vindicator," and additional archiving information.

Below is a review of Tiny Arcade's Tape 103, which includes this game and Paul Thacker's archiving notes for Tape 103.

--------------------

"Vindicator" Review.
By Michael Prosise.
September 1983.

This is an excerpt from a review first published in "The Game Player" column #11 by Michael Prosise in ARCADIAN 5, no. 11 (Sep. 28, 1983): 165.  This review covers Tiny Arcade Tape 3, which has two programs: and "Vindicator" and "Art SHOW."

VINDICATOR, by The Tiny Arcade

VINDICATOR is very similar to the coin-op DEFENDER, and although not as lavish as the coin-op, VINDICATOR provides essentially the same type of play action and entertainment.

In this one-player game from Tiny Arcade, the player has six "lives," in the forms of star fighters that must shoot down five orbiting robot ships, avoiding their lasers and the ground-to-air missiles.

Using the joystick skillfully, one is able to guide his star fighter up or down, fast or slow, and shoot left or right, as he moves across the landscape, just like in DEFENDER.

We liked playing VINDICATOR, and one reason is that it is not a fast-paced game.  Things do not go "flying" around the screen at high speeds, and thus the player does not find him/herself frantically shooting wildly and becoming frustrated.  As in the excellent game OMEGA RACE (see ARCADIAN Vo1. 5, #1, pg. 19), also by Tiny Arcade, the player is given time to think and plan ahead.  We think this is an important part of any game if it is to be enjoyable and satisfying. Sound effects and graphics are quite satisfactory, although there was an annoying, high-frequency buzz in the background at all times.

VINDICATOR is one of the better games to come from Tiny Arcade, but it is apparently no longer available by itself.  It is currently being offered in a package deal with five other programs for $16.95.  Along with VINDICATOR, this one tape includes GAMMA WARS (see ARCADIAN Vol. 5, #1, pg. 127), VIPERIAN (unavailable for review), ART SHOW (review follows), ASTRO TERROR (see ARCADIAN Vol. 5, #1, pg. 19) and CRUNCHER (unavailable for review).

ART SHOW is one of the finest graphic-display programs available for the Astrocade unit.  It contains seven separate and most excellent, full-color graphic programs.  What a great way to show off the power and ability of your Bally Astrocade to others.

Since the GAME PLAYER is not able to include reviews of VIPERIAN and CRUNCHER, it would not be fair to the Tiny Arcade to rate this $16.95 tape overall.  But at less than $3.00 per game, this $16.95 tape of six games looks like it might be a good bargain.

[The review is "Candy Man" is not included here.]

--------------------

Archive Notes:

The announcement that "Vindicator" was archived, along with several other AstroBASIC programs, was announced on July 29, 2022 by Paul Thacker on the Astrocade discussion group on Groups.io, here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/tiny_arcade_tape_103_and/84535683

Here is the excerpted information about "Vindicator:"

"Two copies on tape, no apparent differences, but not byte for byte identical. No title screen. It's a space shooter that looks a bit like Defender. Your ship automatically moves from left to right before wrapping back to the left side of the screen. You can push left or right to slow down or speed up. Push up or down to move up or down. Pull the trigger to fire a beam a short distance in front of your ship. Use the beam to take out five stationary targets, which can fire horizontally in either direction. Avoid rockets moving directly up from the ground. Once you take out all the targets, more will generate. You have five lives to score as many points as possible. I found the rockets frustrating, as they respawn once they hit you or move above your ship, so you can get hit repeatedly when trying to take out targets near the ground."

Thanks for archiving this game, Paul.  I want to make a video of the gameplay of this game, for although it looks like Defender or Scramble in screenshots, it's actually quite different and simple compared to those games.  Well, what are ya gonna do when you're limited to 1.8K or RAM?

Enjoy!

I don't think the name change has something to do with that other Bit Corp. Maybe there was another machine with the same name anywhere? Note that "Wrap Bit" is a tricky change, designed to keep the pronunciation very close to the original "Rabbit".

As for whether or not the Wrap Bit II was actually released... Daniel Young did prompt Fabris to buy "5–10 units for developments and trial distribution" which they would then "forward" to him "within 2 weeks". Is that time for shipping only, or would they still have to produce them? Your files include an advertisement of the Rabbit II in a "LTE/The Retail Computer" magazine. The editors of Personal Computer News magazine got a unit to review. At the very least they had the machine fully designed and produced a bunch of units.

Ah, the sample program that illustrates the Wrap Bit II graphic commands.

Well, GR1 and MODE=<mode number> set some graphic mode (256x192, 16 colors?).

PATTERN seems obvious, it would define an 8x8 bit pattern: PATTERN <pattern number> # <8 comma-separated byte values>

INK=<color number> sets the foreground color, and PLOT <x>,<y> plots a dot on the screen in the specified foreground color.

Given the description given by Daniel Young ("a few flying saucers are moving in the galaxy"), I guess: MOVE(<sprite number>, <x shift>, <y shift>).

Now the real mistery was SPRITE, but after thinking it over and over I think I got it:

SPRITE(<sprite number>, <x>, <y>, <first pattern number>, <color number>) defines and displays a sprite, giving its position, the first in a sequence of FOUR patterns that make up the 16x16 sprite, and its color.

Episode 5 of the Bally Alley Astrocast doesn't cover a game. Chris has left as a co-host, so the review of "The Incredible Wizard" has been pushed to episode 6. Paul and I cover the "Arcadian" newsletter issues 5 and 6 (March and May 1979).  We cover a bit of feedback too. Paul and I discuss eleven letters to the "Arcadian," dating mostly from the spring of 1979.

The Bally Alley Astrocast #5  was originally released six years ago, on October 12, 2016, in the following thread:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/message/14833

The video version of the podcast is now the sixth episode in the "Bally Alley Astrocast Podcast" YouTube playlist, which is here:

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLADcQ67H2uU2CKrEt5s2OS_5t6t4UZdop

The extensive show notes for Astrocast #5, as well as the audio-only version of the podcast, are here:

https://ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com/podcast/bally-alley-astrocast-005-arcadian-newsletter-march-and-may-1979

I uploaded this episode to YouTube last night.  "kidguzzi" listened to the show already this morning and left this feedback, "Another very interesting show.  Thanks!"  I had been a bit worried about this one and I replied with this message:

"I'm glad that you enjoyed this episode that didn't even feature a game.  I listened to it yesterday after I converted the show from the audio-only WAV file to the video I added to YouTube last night.  I hadn't heard the show since its release in 2016 and I wondered if anyone at all was really interested in a podcast episode about a game console that doesn't feature a game.  I hoped that the coverage of the letters to Bob Fabris and the two Arcadian newsletters would carry it through for at least a few people.  I guess that this episode is another example that pushes the Bally Arcade console one step closer toward computer and away from game-console-only system."

The next show, episode 6 of the Bally Alley Astrocast, covers "The Incredible Wizard," the port of the arcade game "Wizard of Wor." Paul and I are joined by our new co-host Michael Di Salvo. Paul and I cover the "Arcadian" newsletter issues 7 and 8 (June and July 1979). Paul and I discuss six letters to the "Arcadian," dating from the spring and summer of 1979.

It has been fun to hear to these episodes of the Astrocast again.  I like the interaction between Paul and me.  I hope that other listeners enjoy the show too.  If you have any feedback that you would like to leave about this episode, then don't let the six year gap between the original release of this show and now stop you from leaving some comments for us.

Have fun!

I added "Snake Snack/Cone Man" by Ken Lill on one Blue Ram BASICart to BallyAlley.com.  These are both Blue Ram BASIC games that require expansion RAM.

https://ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html#Snake_Snack-Cone_Man_BRB_Cart

This 8K cartridge ROM image contains two games written in Blue Ram BASIC 1.1. Just like many other BASICarts, once the menu appears and the player chooses a game, then the cartridge with the games needs to be switched out with the "Blue Ram BASIC" cartridge.  Currently, the Astrocade emulator in MAME doesn't support this feature, so this game can only be played on a real Astrocade.  I burned the cartridge to an EPROM today and it worked fine for me.
